newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland's IRA guerrillas ponder truce call.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland's IRA guerrillas ponder truce call.

text.p: IRA guerrillas were reported to be close to ending a long war against British rule in Northern Ireland so as to win a voice in peace talks.
Politicians and media reports said the outlawed Irish Republican Army (IRA) was likely to accede to a ceasefire call from Gerry Adams, leader of its Sinn Fein political arm.
BBC radio quoted security sources late on Friday as saying a ceasefire was expected soon.
By midnight however, no announcement had been made by the underground army that has fought for 28 years and media reports said it might be several days before the IRA comments publicly.
Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern spoke for nationalists on both sides of the divided island when he welcomed Adams' decision to go to the IRA to seek a fresh cessation of violence.
"I trust and hope that their response will be positive as this would be very good news for all the people of Ireland....
"We must all unite to consolidate peace and to ensure that the gun in Irish politics is silenced for the last time," he said in a statement.

But politicians for the province's 60 per cent Protestant majority, who support British rule, said they suspected any ceasefire would be a rerun of a ruse they said the guerrillas embarked on with their first truce in August 31 1994.
That ceasefire lasted 18 months, ending in February 1996 with a huge bomb in east London.

"Why would I welcome a phoney and tactical cessation of violence by the IRA in order that they can extract further concessions," said Peter Robinson, a member of the British parliament and deputy head of the hardline Democratic Unionists.

"There is very little for (Protestant) Unionists to welcome in the fact that Her Majesty's Government have been prepared to surrender to IRA/Sinn Fein by making the concessions that they (already) have," he told Sky Television.

In a sudden initiative which took London and Dublin by surprise, Adams said on Friday he had urged the IRA leaders to renew their truce. His announcement came after months of political upheaval and guerrilla conflict that had threatened to spill over into communal violence.

Adams signalled he was now satisfied that Britain was committed to holding all-party talks that would not be blocked by Unionist demands for early surrender of IRA arms and which would consider republican demands for a "United Ireland".
"The process of obtaining detail and clarity on these issues has been painstaking but essential," Adams said.
Declaration of a ceasefire paves the way for Sinn Fein to enter full-scale Northern Ireland negotiations that Britain and Ireland say must get under way by mid-September.

But a dark cloud hangs over the talks process which has been struggling during more than a year of acrimony between Protestant and Catholic parties in talks chaired by former U.S.senator George Mitchell.
Unionist parties are angry about British and Irish plans for achieving guerrilla disarmament in the event of a ceasefire.
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, which speaks for most Protestants, says they are too vague. He wants a commitment to guns being handed in at the start of full talks.

Adams said, "I have made it clear over the 18 months since the collapse of the peace process that I would only approach the IRA to restore their cessation if I was confident that their response would be positive."

A Sinn Fein statement said Adams and his chief political lieutenant Martin McGuinness had "provided a detailed report and assessment to the IRA and ...urged the IRA leadership to restore its cessation of August 1994".
"The IRA leadership has assured us that they would respond without delay to our request," Adams said.
